prompt: A processor's control unit is responsible for:

options.text: Coordinating instruction execution through control signals

explanation: The control unit is the conductor. It decodes each instruction and issues the control signals that tell every other unit what to do and when.

why.a: Wrong. Arithmetic is the ALU's job. Control unit and ALU are the two halves of the CPU, and the exam separates them constantly.
why.b: Wrong. Files are held in secondary storage, managed by the operating system.
why.c: Correct. Decode, then sequence the rest of the machine through control signals.
why.d: Wrong. Power management belongs to the power supply and chipset, not to the instruction control path.

prompt: A software engineer optimizes a program by storing frequently used variables in CPU registers instead of RAM. The primary benefit is:
explanation: Registers sit inside the CPU and are reached in a single cycle, while RAM costs tens or hundreds of cycles.

why.a: Wrong, and backwards. There are only a few dozen registers, so capacity falls rather than rises.
why.b: Wrong because of the word ONLY. Less bus traffic is a real side effect, but the PRIMARY benefit is speed.
why.c: Wrong. Registers are the most expensive storage per bit in the whole machine.
why.d: Correct. The variable is already where the ALU needs it, so no memory trip is made.

prompt: Which bus carries information identifying memory locations and I/O device locations?
explanation: Three buses, three jobs: the address bus says WHERE, the data bus carries WHAT, and the control bus says WHEN and WHICH WAY.

why.a: Wrong. The control bus carries timing and command signals such as read and write.
why.b: Wrong. The data bus carries the value itself, once the location has been named.
why.c: Wrong. "Memory bus" is a loose collective term for the whole path, not the line that carries locations.
why.d: Correct. Location information travels on the address bus, and its width sets how much memory can be addressed.

prompt: An autonomous robot continuously performs sensor processing and actuator control. Which organizational component primarily coordinates these activities?
explanation: The keyword is COORDINATES. Whenever a stem asks which component sequences or directs activity, the answer is the control unit.

why.a: Correct. Coordination and sequencing is the control unit's defining role.
why.b: Wrong. The ALU computes results when told to, it does not decide the order of work.
why.c: Wrong. Registers hold operands and results. Storage is not coordination.
why.d: Wrong. Cache speeds up access to recently used data, which is a performance aid and not a controller.

prompt: A motherboard manufacturer introduces a faster bus system, enabling quicker communication among components. This enhancement belongs to:
explanation: A faster bus changes how components are interconnected and how quickly they talk. No instruction changes, so nothing programmer-visible changes.

why.a: Wrong. Architecture would mean a change to the instruction set or the programmer-visible model, and there is none here.
why.b: Wrong. No instruction was added, removed or re-encoded.
why.c: Wrong. Data representation is about encoding numbers and characters, untouched by bus speed.
why.d: Correct. Interconnection and speed are organization.

prompt: Which statement regarding ROM is correct?

options.text: ROM is mainly used for temporary program execution.
ROM loses contents after power failure.

explanation: ROM is read-only and non-volatile, which is why the boot firmware lives there and survives a power cut.

why.a: Wrong. Temporary working storage is RAM's job. ROM holds code that must persist.
why.b: Correct. Firmware such as the BIOS is held permanently in ROM.
why.c: Wrong. Refreshing is a DRAM requirement, because DRAM stores charge in capacitors that leak.
why.d: Wrong, and the direct opposite. ROM is non-volatile, so its contents survive power loss.

prompt: Why is cache memory generally constructed using SRAM rather than DRAM?

options.text: SRAM offers faster access without refresh operations.

explanation: SRAM holds each bit in a flip-flop, so it is fast and needs no refresh. Cache exists to be fast, so it pays SRAM's price.

why.a: Correct. Speed with no refresh cycles stealing access time.
why.b: Wrong, and backwards. SRAM uses about six transistors per bit against DRAM's one transistor and one capacitor, so it costs far more.
why.c: Wrong. SRAM is volatile, like DRAM. It loses everything when power goes.
why.d: Wrong. DRAM is the denser technology, which is exactly why main memory is DRAM.

prompt: Which architectural feature most directly contributes to reducing the average instruction execution time without increasing clock frequency?
explanation: Average access time is hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty. Raise the hit rate and the average falls, with the clock untouched.

why.a: Wrong. Monitor resolution is a display property and does not touch instruction timing.
why.b: Wrong. Disk capacity is about how much you can store, not how fast instructions execute.
why.c: Wrong. A bigger ROM holds more firmware. It does not speed up running code.
why.d: Correct. Fewer misses means fewer long trips to main memory.

prompt: Which of the following correctly orders memory from fastest to slowest?

options.text: Registers → Cache → Main Memory → Secondary Storage
Cache → Registers → Main Memory → Hard Disk

explanation: Registers, cache, main memory, secondary storage. Learn this ladder once and it answers a whole family of questions: speed and cost per bit fall together as capacity rises.

why.a: Wrong twice. Registers must come before cache, and RAM is faster than an SSD, not slower.
why.b: Correct. The standard hierarchy, top to bottom.
why.c: Wrong. Cache sits between registers and main memory, not below main memory.
why.d: Wrong. The last two are in order, but registers are faster than cache, so the first pair is swapped.

prompt: Which combination correctly matches memory type with volatility?
explanation: Only flash keeps its contents without power. DRAM, SRAM and the cache built from SRAM are all volatile.

why.a: Correct. Flash holds charge on a floating gate, so a USB drive still has your files tomorrow.
why.b: Wrong. DRAM is volatile, and it does not even hold data for a full second without refreshing.
why.c: Wrong. SRAM is volatile too. It needs no refresh, but it does need power.
why.d: Wrong. Cache is built from SRAM, so it is volatile as well.

prompt: Which statement correctly explains memory hierarchy?

options.text: Main memory is faster than registers.
Every memory level has identical speed.
Higher levels are faster, smaller, and more expensive per bit.
Lower levels are faster than upper levels.

explanation: Climbing the hierarchy, speed rises, size falls and cost per bit rises. All three move together, which is why the pyramid has its shape.

why.a: Wrong, and inverted. Registers are the fastest storage in the machine.
why.b: Wrong. If every level were equally fast there would be no reason to have a hierarchy at all.
why.c: Correct, and all three properties are stated together.
why.d: Wrong, and inverted again. Lower means larger, cheaper and slower.

prompt: A computer architect argues that registers should be larger than cache memory. Why is this argument incorrect?

options.text: Registers are intended for only the most immediate processor operations.

explanation: Registers exist to hold the handful of values in use RIGHT NOW. Adding more would need wider instruction fields to name them and would slow the register file down.

why.a: Wrong. Virtual memory is a main memory and disk mechanism. Registers are physical CPU storage.
why.b: Correct. Their job is the immediate working set, so a small, very fast file is the right design.
why.c: Wrong. Secondary storage is disk and SSD, at the very bottom of the hierarchy.
why.d: Wrong, and plainly false. Registers are the FASTEST storage there is.

prompt: Which memory characteristic is most critical for real-time control systems?
explanation: Real-time means a deadline must be met EVERY time. Predictability matters as much as raw speed, since a fast average with an occasional long stall still misses deadlines.

why.a: Wrong. Cost is a business constraint, not a timing guarantee.
why.b: Correct. Note the word PREDICTABLE. This is why some real-time designs prefer tightly coupled memory over an unpredictable cache.
why.c: Wrong. A control system's working set is usually small. Capacity is not the binding constraint.
why.d: Wrong. Density is a manufacturing property, and it says nothing about worst-case timing.

prompt: Why is secondary storage unsuitable for direct CPU execution of instructions?

options.text: It has significantly higher access latency than primary memory.

explanation: Disk latency is measured in milliseconds against nanoseconds for RAM, a gap of about a million to one. That is why programs are loaded into main memory before they run.

why.a: Wrong. Every level of the hierarchy stores binary data, so this cannot be the distinguishing reason.
why.b: Correct. The latency gap is the whole reason for loading before executing.
why.c: Wrong. Non-volatility is an ADVANTAGE of secondary storage, not an obstacle to execution.
why.d: Wrong. Logical addressing is a translation scheme, and it does not prevent execution.

prompt: Which statement best summarizes the fundamental trade-off underlying modern computer memory hierarchy?

options.text: All memory technologies have similar speed and cost.
Slower memories always consume more power than faster memories.
Faster memories generally provide larger capacities at lower cost.
Faster memories are typically smaller and more expensive per bit, while slower memories provide larger capacities at lower cost.

explanation: You cannot have fast, large and cheap at once. The hierarchy exists to buy the ILLUSION of all three by keeping hot data high and cold data low.

why.a: Wrong. If speed and cost were similar everywhere, one flat memory would do and there would be no hierarchy.
why.b: Wrong. "Always" overstates it, and slower technologies such as disk and DRAM are generally cheaper per bit in power terms too.
why.c: Wrong, and exactly inverted. Fast memory is small and expensive.
why.d: Correct, and it states both halves of the trade-off.

prompt: Which statement best distinguishes SRAM from DRAM?

options.text: SRAM stores data using flip-flops whereas DRAM stores data using capacitors.
SRAM requires periodic refreshing while DRAM does not.

explanation: One structural fact explains everything else: flip-flops hold their state, so SRAM is fast and needs no refresh but costs many transistors. Capacitors leak, so DRAM must be refreshed but packs far more bits per chip.

why.a: Correct, and it is the root fact from which the rest follows.
why.b: Wrong, and inverted. SRAM is the faster of the two, which is why cache uses it.
why.c: Wrong, and inverted. DRAM is the one that must be refreshed, and the D stands for dynamic.
why.d: Wrong. DRAM is volatile, and it loses data in milliseconds without refreshing.

prompt: A computer engineer claims that increasing cache memory always eliminates processor-memory performance bottlenecks. Which statement best evaluates this claim?

options.text: It is correct only when DRAM is removed.
It is incorrect because cache cannot eliminate all memory access delays.
It is correct because cache replaces main memory.
It is always correct because cache operates at processor speed.

explanation: Compulsory misses still happen, large working sets still overflow, and a bigger cache is itself slower to search. Cache narrows the gap, it never closes it.

why.a: Wrong. Removing DRAM would leave nowhere to back the cache from, so the machine could not run at all.
why.b: Correct. Misses are inevitable, so some delay always remains.
why.c: Wrong. Cache SUPPLEMENTS main memory, holding copies. It does not replace it.
why.d: Wrong. Cache is fast, but the claim fails on "always": a miss still costs a full trip to main memory.

prompt: A processor spends considerable time waiting for data despite having a large cache. Which phenomenon is primarily responsible?
explanation: Processor speed has grown far faster than memory speed for decades. That widening gap is the memory wall, and cache only softens it.

why.a: Wrong. Address aliasing is two addresses referring to one location, a correctness issue rather than a speed one.
why.b: Wrong. Register spilling is the compiler running out of registers and pushing values to memory. It is a contributor at most, not the phenomenon named here.
why.c: Correct. The processor-memory speed gap, which is exactly what the stem describes.
why.d: Wrong. Bus inversion is a signalling trick for cutting switching power, unrelated to waiting for data.

prompt: Which component stores the address of the memory location currently being accessed?
explanation: MAR holds WHERE, MDR holds WHAT. The pair is worth memorising together, because the paper sets both.

why.a: Correct. The Memory Address Register drives the address bus.
why.b: Wrong. The MDR holds the DATA travelling to or from that address.
why.c: Wrong, and the near miss. The Program Counter holds the address of the NEXT INSTRUCTION, not of the location being accessed right now.
why.d: Wrong. The Instruction Register holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.

prompt: A processor repeatedly accesses the same instruction during program execution. The improved execution speed primarily results from which memory hierarchy principle?
explanation: Temporal is about TIME: the SAME location used again soon. Spatial is about PLACE: NEARBY locations used next. The word "repeatedly" settles it.

why.a: Wrong. Spatial locality concerns neighbouring addresses, and the word ONLY makes it worse.
why.b: Correct. The same item reused shortly after, which is a cache hit.
why.c: Wrong. Virtual addressing is an address translation mechanism, not a locality principle.
why.d: Wrong. Sequential consistency is a memory ordering model for multiprocessors.

prompt: A memory technology provides higher density but lower speed than SRAM. Which technology is being described?
explanation: One transistor and one capacitor per bit against SRAM's six transistors. That is why DRAM packs more bits per chip and runs slower.

why.a: Wrong. ROM is read-only, so it is not the read-write main memory the comparison implies.
why.b: Wrong. EEPROM is non-volatile and much slower to write, used for firmware rather than main memory.
why.c: Wrong. Registers are the fastest and least dense storage in the machine, the opposite of this description.
why.d: Correct. Denser and slower than SRAM, which is why main memory is DRAM and cache is SRAM.

prompt: Which memory level has the highest cost per bit?
explanation: Cost per bit rises as you climb the hierarchy, so the top level is the dearest. Registers are built from the fastest logic and sit inside the processor die.

why.a: Wrong. An SSD is near the bottom, cheap per bit and large.
why.b: Correct. Highest in the hierarchy, therefore highest cost per bit.
why.c: Wrong. Main memory is DRAM, far cheaper per bit than the SRAM and logic above it.
why.d: Wrong. Hard disk is the cheapest per bit of the four.

prompt: Which statement correctly describes virtual memory?

options.text: It allows programs to execute using an address space larger than physical memory.

explanation: Virtual memory gives each program a large logical address space, with pages moved between RAM and disk as needed.

why.a: Wrong. Cache and virtual memory sit at different levels and coexist.
why.b: Wrong. No RAM is added. The illusion of more is created using disk, and the word PHYSICALLY gives this away.
why.c: Wrong, and inverted. Page faults are the MECHANISM of virtual memory, not something it removes.
why.d: Correct. An address space larger than the physical memory installed.

prompt: Which memory characteristic primarily determines how much information can be stored in a memory device?
explanation: Capacity is HOW MUCH. Access time and transfer rate are HOW FAST, and volatility is WHETHER IT SURVIVES power loss.

why.a: Wrong. Access time is the delay before data arrives, a speed measure.
why.b: Correct. Capacity is the total amount that can be held.
why.c: Wrong. Transfer rate is bits per second, another speed measure.
why.d: Wrong. Volatility says whether contents survive without power, not how much fits.

prompt: A memory module has an access time of 60 ns and a cycle time of 90 ns. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Access time is longer than cycle time.
Cycle time has no practical significance.
Consecutive accesses must be separated by at least 90 ns.
A new memory operation can begin every 60 ns.

explanation: Access time is how long until the data arrives, 60 ns here. Cycle time is how long until the memory can START AGAIN, 90 ns here, because it needs 30 ns of recovery. Cycle time is always the larger of the two.

why.a: Wrong, and contradicted by the figures given: 60 is less than 90.
why.b: Wrong. Cycle time sets the maximum sustainable rate, which is very practical indeed.
why.c: Correct. The next access can only begin after the full 90 ns cycle.
why.d: Wrong, and the trap. 60 ns is when the DATA ARRIVES, not when the next operation may start.

prompt: A workload frequently accesses neighboring memory locations after accessing a particular location. Which locality principle is being demonstrated?
explanation: NEIGHBOURING locations means space, so this is spatial locality. It is why cache fetches a whole block rather than a single word, and why array traversal is fast.

why.a: Wrong. There is no such principle. It is invented to sound like virtual memory.
why.b: Wrong. Random access is the ABSENCE of locality, which is the worst case for a cache.
why.c: Wrong, and the near miss. Temporal locality is the same location reused over TIME, while this stem says neighbouring.
why.d: Correct. Nearby addresses accessed next.
